name: PT Astra Otoparts Tbk

frontmatter.title: Astra Otoparts - an autoparts franchise priced as a break-up
frontmatter.summary: An Astra-controlled autoparts maker whose share price is close to the sum of its net cash and the book value of its Japanese joint-venture stakes, so the operating business trades at a small multiple of its cash earnings. Earnings are compounding on the strongest car-market recovery in years and the dividend is covered. We initiate at BUY.
thesis: The share price is close to net cash plus the book value of the associate and joint-venture stakes, so the operating autoparts business is being valued at a small fraction of its cash earnings and replacement cost.
Segment mix is shifting toward manufacturing; revenue is growing at a double-digit pace but gross margin is lower, and our base case holds the observed margin rather than assuming a recovery.

The local-content step-up is written for electric vehicles, a small share of revenue today, so we treat it as a free option rather than the reason to own the shares; the carrier is the aftermarket distribution network and the OEM scale behind it.
Cash conversion is strong, the balance sheet carries net cash rather than net debt, and the board has paid out roughly half of earnings through the cycle.
The main risk is a sharp fourth-quarter car-sales slowdown plus imported Chinese components compressing aftermarket margins further; both are in our bear case.

catalysts.event: Gaikindo November wholesales data and the run-rate into the year-end target
Higher minimum local-content threshold takes effect for battery electric vehicles
FY2026 audited results and the board's dividend recommendation
Annual general meeting approving the FY2026 final dividend

open_items: IDX board and notation status unverified — no IDX announcement or KSEI registry extract held; no entry or exit assumption in this report depends on it.

blocks.text: We initiate coverage of PT Astra Otoparts at BUY with a twelve-month target of Rp4,837, a total return of 58.0% from the Rp3,220 price in our data pack. The target is the weighted output of a free-cash-flow DCF at fifty per cent, a P/E cross-check at thirty and an EV/EBITDA cross-check at twenty, with the base case at Rp4,776 and the probability-weighted scenario value at Rp4,837.

The variant view is about what the market is actually charging for. At the current capitalisation of IDR15,519.5bn, the company is valued at little more than the sum of its balance-sheet liquidity and the carrying value of its stakes in Denso Indonesia, GS Battery, Akebono Brake, Kayaba and a dozen smaller component ventures. The balance sheet at 30 September 2026 holds cash of IDR5,087.8bn against total borrowings of IDR560.5bn, and the associates and joint ventures carry at IDR2,327.7bn and IDR5,123.6bn respectively at that date [S3]. Those stakes earned IDR1,176.9bn of equity-accounted profit in FY2025, so they are not a dormant asset [S5]. Strip the cash and the stakes out and the market is ascribing a multiple of barely two times cash earnings to a business that generates IDR1,853.2bn of EBITDA on IDR19,906.8bn of revenue — cheap enough that the debate is about whether the discount should exist at all, not about the price of the operating franchise.

The operating evidence is not gloomy. Nine-month revenue to September reached IDR17,021.9bn, with manufacturing revenue of IDR9,180.5bn and trading revenue of IDR7,841.3bn, and profit attributable to shareholders of IDR1,799.9bn [S3]. Management describes the growth as demand-led, from original-equipment component volumes across cars, motorcycles and commercial vehicles and from a fuller aftermarket range sold through the retail network [S2]. The company also guided for growth above the industry rate in 2027 [S7].

What moves the value is therefore narrow and identifiable. First, national car wholesales: Gaikindo recorded 679,020 units in the first nine months and targets 850,000 for the full year [S8]. Second, gross margin mix: manufacturing carries a far lower margin than trading, so the faster the manufacturing line grows the more group margin dilutes [S3]. Third, equity-accounted income from the joint ventures, which is close to half of pretax profit — IDR1,176.9bn on IDR2,639.5bn — and is the single largest reason our DCF value sits above the market price [S5]. We take each in turn below.

The stock is not without reasons to be cheap. The free float is 19.9% with Astra International holding 80 per cent of the shares, and the stock trades about IDR11.4bn a day [S0]. A minority holder is buying a controlled company's cash flows at a discount, and that discount is the risk as much as the opportunity.

Astra Otoparts makes and distributes parts for cars and motorcycles through two reportable segments. The trading segment buys, warehouses and distributes replacement parts through a network of 49 main dealers, 28 sales offices and more than 15,000 independent parts shops, supplemented by 673 modern retail outlets trading as Shop & Drive, Super Shop & Drive, Astra Otoservice, Shop & Bike and Aspira Motoquick [S2]. The manufacturing segment supplies original equipment to vehicle assemblers and the original-equipment service channel, through owned plants and through joint ventures with Japanese component makers [S4].

The mix matters more than the headline. In FY2025 the trading segment booked IDR9,340.8bn of external revenue and manufacturing IDR10,565.9bn, so manufacturing is the larger half [S4]. Trading earned a gross margin several times the manufacturing margin, however, and manufacturing reaches that revenue on a base that also includes intersegment sales [S4]. The segment growing fastest is therefore the one that dilutes group margin, and the nine-month results show exactly that [S3].

The product range is broad rather than deep in any single category: batteries, chains and filters, rubber and metal components, jacks and tools, plastic components, pistons, wheel rims, frame chassis and transmission parts [S0]. Several subsidiaries act as export production bases for Japanese, American and European customers, and the group sells into more than 50 countries [S4]. Electrification is being handled as an extension rather than a replacement: management argues that shock absorbers, brakes and many general parts do not change between combustion and electric vehicles, while separately developing electric-vehicle-specific components and a charging business of 71 Astra Otopower units [S7].

The strategic plan for 2027 is explicit: grow above the industry rate, add around 30 modern retail stores, deepen the aftermarket range and the digital Astra Otoshop channel, and expand electric-vehicle components and charging infrastructure [S7]. That is a continuation of the current model rather than a new one, which is why we model it as revenue growth on a stable margin rather than as a margin story [S7].

Ownership is central to how the equity should be valued. PT Astra International Tbk owns 80 per cent of the shares and the balance is in public hands [S4]. The controlling group is also the customer base: Astra Honda Motor and Astra Daihatsu Motor take a large share of manufacturing output, which we return to in the governance section [S5]. Below the listed company sit the consolidated manufacturing subsidiaries and, alongside them, the equity-accounted ventures — Denso Indonesia at an effective stake in the mid-twenties, and GS Battery, Akebono Brake Astra, Kayaba Indonesia and Inti Ganda Perdana at or near half ownership [S5].

The demand pool is Indonesian vehicle production and the vehicle parc. Car wholesales reached 679,020 units in the first nine months of 2026, and Gaikindo targets 850,000 units for the full year, having trimmed that from an earlier and more optimistic figure [S8]. The motorcycle market is larger and steadier: sales passed the five million mark by September and the industry association expects a full-year range whose upper end is 6.7 million units [S9]. Astra's own framing, in its annual report, is that four-wheeler demand was the volatile part of the market while two-wheelers were relatively stagnant [S4].

The arithmetic of the target is worth stating plainly because it drives the fourth quarter. To reach 850,000 units after 679,020 in nine months, the industry needs a fourth-quarter run-rate well below the year-to-date pace [S8]. That is not a forecast of collapse, and it does not require a weak market; it does mean that the year-on-year growth rate in the fourth quarter will be much lower than the year-to-date rate, and we have built that into the revenue path rather than extrapolating nine months of growth.

Regulation matters, but less than the headline suggests, and we scale it to the revenue it can reach. The minimum domestic content requirement is set by Perpres 79/2023 and steps to 60 per cent for 2027 to 2029 and to eighty per cent from 2030 — but the rule is written for battery electric vehicles, not for the internal-combustion content that is the overwhelming majority of this company's revenue [S13]. The company treats electrification as an extension of the existing range rather than a replacement, with a charging business of 71 units and components common to both powertrains [S7]. So the local-content step is a real but small option: it can convert imported electric-vehicle content into addressable demand for a maker with existing plants and original- equipment qualification, provided the local industry can scale, and the same policy discussion warns that a threshold without enforcement and without demand simply raises assemblers' costs [S13]. We therefore do not treat it as the industry's dominant variable; the car cycle and the aftermarket import threat are larger.

Competition is two-sided. On the original-equipment side the barriers are qualification cycles, tooling investment and quality consistency; the relationship is sticky but the customer holds the pricing power, which is why manufacturing margins are thin [S4]. On the aftermarket side the barriers are distribution density and brand, and here the threat is imported product, particularly from China, which the industry association acknowledges as the sector's central competitive challenge even as it argues that the electric transition does not eliminate the parts market [S12]. The company's own answer is authenticity, quality and service reliability rather than price [S4].

Our view of the moat is that it is real but narrow, and that it sits in distribution rather than in technology. The parts-shop network, the dealer relationships and the retail footprint are expensive to replicate and give the trading segment a gross margin several times the manufacturing margin [S3]. The manufacturing side has scale and long-standing Japanese partners, but it earns a supplier's return, and the joint ventures that hold the best technology are not consolidated [S5]. That is why we value the operating business on cash flow with a fade rather than as a compounder with a widening moat, and why the associate portfolio is carried at book rather than capitalised at a growth multiple.

Autoparts economics split cleanly between the original-equipment channel and the replacement
aftermarket. Original-equipment supply is a volume business with thin margins, long qualification
cycles and annual price-downs negotiated by the assembler. The aftermarket is a distribution business:
margins are wider, demand is tied to the vehicle parc rather than to new sales, and the constraint is
shelf space and logistics reach rather than engineering. Companies that own both channels use the
original-equipment relationship to seed brand acceptance and the aftermarket network to earn the
return. Vehicle electrification shifts the component list but leaves much of the chassis, braking and
suspension content in place.

Five forces, briefly. Supplier power is moderate and partly internal, since several joint ventures are also suppliers [S5]. Buyer power is high in original equipment and lower in the aftermarket [S4]. Threat of new entrants is low in qualified original equipment and moderate in imported aftermarket parts [S12]. Substitutes are the electric powertrain, which removes engine and transmission content but not the rest [S12]. Rivalry is high and rising, with the trading segment competing on range and authenticity and manufacturing competing on cost and delivery [S4].

External influences are mostly macro. A weaker rupiah raises the cost of imported raw materials and finished parts, and the house macro deck projects the exchange rate at 18,350 to the dollar in 2027 [S0]. Interest rates matter less here than for most Indonesian names because the company holds net cash, but they matter for the cost of the working capital that funds inventory and receivables [S5]. The demand cycle is the swing factor, and it is cyclical rather than structural: the parc keeps growing even when new sales stall [S4].

The historical record is one of slow top-line growth and steady profitability until this year. Revenue moved from IDR18,579.9bn in FY2022 to IDR19,906.8bn in FY2025, a compound rate in the low single digits, while gross profit rose from IDR2,689.3bn to IDR3,366.2bn as the trading mix improved [S5]. Operating profit over the same span went from IDR957.4bn to IDR1,265.9bn [S5]. Then 2026 broke the pattern: nine-month revenue of IDR17,021.9bn and gross profit of IDR2,649.6bn are both well ahead of the comparable period, and profit attributable to shareholders reached IDR1,799.9bn [S3].

The first restatement a reader needs is depreciation. The data pack carries a D&A charge that is a small fraction of what the accounts show, because Indonesian filings present the cash-flow statement on the direct method and the depreciation sits in the notes rather than on a face line. From the notes, total depreciation and amortisation was IDR529.9bn in FY2022, IDR525.8bn in FY2023, IDR562.7bn in FY2024 and IDR587.2bn in FY2025, and IDR458.3bn in the first nine months of 2026 [S5][S6][S11]. We feed those into the model, which rebuilds EBITDA: FY2025 EBITDA is IDR1,853.2bn, an EBITDA margin of 9.3%, not the roughly seven per cent a pack-based calculation would show. Every margin statement in this report uses the restated figure.

The second structural point is that operating profit is not where the earnings are. In FY2025 the group earned IDR1,265.9bn of operating profit but IDR2,639.5bn of pretax profit, because below the operating result sit IDR1,162.7bn of non-operating income, of which IDR1,176.9bn is the equity-accounted share of associates and joint ventures, and IDR248.4bn of finance income [S5]. We model that equity income explicitly as an other non-operating item at IDR1,650.7bn, annualising a nine-month share-of-associates line that grew strongly year-on-year [S3]. Without it the model would understate earnings by close to half. The line is carried at its pre-tax equivalent so that it bears no tax: the LK deducts the associates' profit from the tax base because it arrives already taxed at the investee, and the model reproduces that by grossing the exempt share up at the operating rate, which leaves FY2026E parent net profit at IDR2,424.7bn and EPS at Rp503 rather than the roughly one-tenth lower figures a model that taxed the associate income a second time would print [S5].

Our forecast for FY2026 is revenue of IDR22,630.0bn, growth of 13.7%, built from the nine-month actual plus a fourth quarter growing more slowly than the year to date because of the Gaikindo arithmetic above [S8]. Gross margin is assumed at 15.6%, essentially the nine-month outcome, which is below the FY2025 level because manufacturing is now the faster-growing segment [S3]. Selling and administrative costs are held at 10.0% of revenue against a nine-month outcome slightly below that, leaving room for wage inflation and the planned store additions [S7]. The FY2025 comparative is the LK's own: selling costs of IDR1,054.5bn plus general and administrative costs of IDR1,072.3bn on net revenue of IDR19,906.8bn [S5]. The model's FY2025 opex line of IDR2,100.3bn is the data pack's and sits below that LK sum, so the restated FY2025 EBITDA of IDR1,853.2bn is slightly above the figure the LK lines imply (gross profit less selling and G&A plus D&A); the gap is in the history and is not carried into the forecast ratio we apply [S5]. The result is FY2026 operating profit of IDR1,267.3bn and EBITDA of IDR1,885.1bn, an EBITDA margin of 8.3% — below FY2025 not because we are cautious but because the mix and the realised gross margin say so.

Cash flow and the balance sheet are the strongest part of the story. Free cash flow to the firm was IDR1,184.9bn in FY2025 after capital expenditure of IDR544.4bn, and net profit converted to cash with little left in working capital [S5]. The nine-month capex figure of IDR445.6bn is running at a similar proportion of revenue [S3]. Working capital is modest at 7.0% of revenue, though it rose in the September balance sheet as payables and inventories built with manufacturing volume [S3]. Cash was IDR4,530.3bn against total debt of IDR597.5bn at the last year-end, and the September position is stronger still: cash and cash equivalents of IDR5,087.8bn against total borrowings of IDR560.5bn [S3].

One forecast convention needs stating here because it is visible in the valuation and not in the five-year table. Capex is held at the observed proportion of revenue through FY2030E, then rises to 4.1% of revenue by FY2035E. That is not a view that the company will become more capital-hungry in the ordinary sense; it is the terminal fade, explained in section four, which sets the return on new capital in the terminal year to the cost of capital instead of leaving the observed near-zero net reinvestment to compound forever [S5][S3]. The explicit years a reader can check against the company's own guidance are unchanged.

Earnings quality screens pass. The accruals ratio, measured as net profit less operating cash flow over average total assets, has been low in each of the last three years and was under two per cent in FY2025, so reported profit is being converted into cash rather than sitting in working capital [S5]. Working capital grew with volume rather than ahead of it, and neither of the usual divergence flags is present [S5]. The one flag that would matter at another company — related-party intensity — is present and large, at 34.8% of revenue and a similar share of purchases, but it is disclosed, reflected in the segment margins and structural to the Astra ecosystem [S5]. We treat it as a governance discount rather than as a manipulation signal, and discuss it in section six.

Capital allocation is conservative and predictable. The board paid a final FY2025 dividend of IDR819.4bn and declared a FY2026 interim of IDR349.5bn, and the payout has run near half of earnings [S3]. With capex at a low proportion of revenue and net cash on the balance sheet, the dividend is covered by free cash flow through the explicit forecast even in a weaker year, and the group has not needed capital markets since listing [S5].

We use a discounted free cash flow to the firm as the primary method, with a P/E cross-check and an EV/EBITDA cross-check. The reason is structural: this is an asset-backed industrial with low, observable capital intensity and a separately identifiable non-operating asset pool, so cash flow is the honest measure, while earnings multiples anchor the answer to what comparable parts businesses trade at. A sum-of-the-parts would also be defensible, but the operating segments share plants, customers and working capital, so a segment-level DCF would be false precision.

The cost of capital is built from the house macro deck: a rupiah risk-free rate of 7.4%, a sovereign default spread of 1.6%, a mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2% and a country risk premium of 2.5%, applied to an unlevered beta of 0.90, the industry default, since the company carries almost no debt and its own regression history is short. The result is a cost of equity of 12.0% and a WACC of 11.9%, inside the house band of eleven to thirteen per cent for rupiah names. Debt is 3.5% of the capital structure because the company holds net cash, so the WACC is effectively the cost of equity.

The tax line in the DCF is the operating rate, not the group's blended rate, and that distinction is worth stating because it is the one place where a consolidated number misleads. The LK's tax charge of IDR291.7bn is struck on pretax profit of IDR2,639.5bn after deducting the share of associates' net profit of IDR1,176.9bn, which arrives already taxed and is modelled outside EBIT [S5]. The rate borne by the operating business is therefore 19.9%, close to the theoretical rate on consolidated profit, and that is what the model applies to EBIT; taxing EBIT at the group's lower blended rate would overstate free cash flow and the target [S5].

The DCF produces an enterprise value of IDR12,047.4bn and an equity value per share of Rp4,875, with the terminal value accounting for 44.2% of the total, within the normal range for a ten-year explicit forecast. Three things drive that number and each is sourced. The explicit-period free cash flow grows from IDR769.9bn in FY2026E to IDR1,120.7bn in FY2035E on the revenue path set out in section three. The reinvestment need is low through those years: capex runs at 2.6% of revenue against D&A of 2.7%, so most of operating profit converts to cash.

The terminal value is where the growth has to be paid for, and we state the identity the house card requires: growth equals the reinvestment rate times the return on incremental capital. Through the forecast years the observed capex and working-capital path reinvests a shrinking share of NOPAT while revenue compounds, an implied incremental return far above anything an autoparts supplier sustains. We therefore fade it. From FY2031E capex rises to 4.1% of revenue by FY2035E, so that the terminal reinvestment rate — capex of IDR1,486.2bn less D&A of IDR1,012.7bn plus the working-capital build of IDR98.1bn, measured against terminal NOPAT — equals the growth rate of 4.0% divided by the cost of capital of 11.9% [S5][S3]. The terminal return on new capital is therefore the WACC, not the near-triple-digit incremental return the unfaded path implied. That is the fade the compounder card demands of a supplier whose moat section two calls real but narrow, and it is why the terminal value is the share of enterprise value shown above rather than the half a no-fade DCF would produce. The terminal growth rate itself stays at 4.0%, below the house cap and below the growth of the car parc, because the fade belongs in the reinvestment rate rather than in a growth rate cut to fit it.

The equity bridge is where this valuation differs from a simple operating-business DCF, and it is struck on the 30 September 2026 balance sheet the engine uses rather than the last year-end. To the enterprise value we add the net cash position: cash and cash equivalents of IDR5,087.8bn against total borrowings of IDR560.5bn, so cash exceeds debt and the net balance is positive and is added, not subtracted [S3]. We then deduct non-controlling interests of IDR1,245.8bn and add the carrying value of the associate and joint-venture investments at the same date, IDR2,327.7bn and IDR5,123.6bn [S3]. That treatment is the neutral one: the stakes earned IDR1,176.9bn last year, so book capitalises them on a single-digit multiple of their income, below the 8.0 times we apply to the group's own earnings and far below the peer median, and a buyer paying book is not paying up for them [S5]. Marking them up to that earnings multiple is the bull case's job, not the base case's, and we do not source a private-market fair value we cannot audit. Their size is why section five stresses the book rather than treating it as unimpeachable.

The bridge carries one more owned asset the operating cash flow does not value. Investment properties of IDR714.2bn sit on the 30 September 2026 balance sheet at carrying value; the rental income they earn is reported in the other-income line below EBIT, so the free cash flow we discount from operating profit does not capture it, and we add the asset at book rather than capitalising the rent separately [S3]. That is the same convention we apply to the associate and joint-venture stakes, and it is deliberately the conservative end of the treatment: book, not an appraised value.

Both cross-checks now sit below the DCF, the EV/EBITDA leg only marginally and the P/E leg by about a fifth, and the reason is knowable rather than mysterious. The P/E cross-check applies 8.0 times, the blend of the peer median and the company's own five-year average, to trailing parent earnings, giving Rp3,674, which is -24.6% against the DCF. The EV/EBITDA cross-check applies 6.2 times to trailing EBITDA of IDR1,853.2bn, which is the restated figure built on the LK's depreciation charge rather than the pack's, giving Rp4,744, or -2.7% against the DCF [S5]. The P/E cross-check capitalises parent earnings at a peer multiple that already embeds the market's current discount for Indonesian small and mid caps, and it is the leg that carries the associate income inside the metric; the EV/EBITDA leg is the closer of the two because it is struck on the restated operating profit and does not depend on the associate line at all.

We have therefore kept the weights rather than re-weighting toward the answer we prefer, and we flag the consequence: the target sits above both cross-checks, and a reader who does not accept the DCF's cash conversion should use the cross-check range as the honest downside.

The sensitivity tables show what matters, and they run in the right direction now that the terminal value is faded. A one percentage point change in the terminal growth rate moves the DCF value by more than a one point change in the WACC, because the terminal value is a large share of the answer; among the operating drivers a one point change in gross margin moves the target more than a one point change in revenue growth, since margin flows straight through to operating profit while growth also drags capex and working capital. The associate income line matters less to the DCF, because we carry the stakes at book rather than capitalising their earnings, but it matters a great deal to the P/E cross-check and therefore to the blended target.

What today's price implies is the most useful test, and the engine runs it explicitly: at Rp3,220 the reverse DCF solves to an implied FY2027E revenue growth rate of -14.8% on the same free-cash-flow model that produces our value, so the share price requires revenue to fall for a decade [S3]. There are only two readings. Either the market is wrong about the operating business, or it is not valuing the operating business at all — it is paying for net cash and the private stakes at a discount and ascribing little to a controlled company's cash flows. The evidence favours the second as the mechanism and the first as the mispricing: the discount on private stakes and cash is real, but it cannot explain an implied decline of that size when the nine-month revenue actual was IDR17,021.9bn, up strongly year on year [S3]. We carry the stakes and net cash at book in the bridge, which is the neutral treatment, and we show the discounted reading in section five rather than pretending it does not exist [S5].

The multiple-survival test is the discipline we apply to any DCF: what exit multiple does the terminal value imply, and would a rational buyer pay it? With the fade in place the test now passes on its own terms. The terminal value on the FY2035E EBITDA of IDR3,125.4bn implies an exit of just under five times, and the same on FY2036E EBITDA, the year the terminal cash flow belongs to — below the 6.2 times the peer set trades at and below the DCF's own starting EV/EBITDA, but above the roughly two and a half times the market ascribes to the operating business today once net cash and the stakes are stripped out. We state that plainly: the DCF does assume a re-rating from the level the market applies, and the re-rating is the mispricing the investment case rests on, not a hidden assumption. That is the arithmetic consequence of paying for growth through reinvestment rather than through an unfaded cash flow: a buyer at that exit is paying for a business whose return on new capital has fallen to the cost of capital, which is what a narrow-moat supplier at 4.0% growth should be worth. An earlier draft of this section reported the test backwards and left the terminal value unfaded; both are corrected here, and the correction is the reason the DCF value is lower than it was.

The peer set deserves the disclosure the table gives it. It is a heterogeneous bucket, not a clean comp set: it contains two-wheel and four-wheel distributors, a battery and electric-vehicle platform with no meaningful earnings, and holding companies whose multiples are struck on different business mixes, and the P/E spread between its cheapest and dearest member is very wide [S0]. We compute the multiple as the blend of the peer median and the company's own multi-year average, so a single outlier cannot set the leg, but a reader should treat both cross-checks as order-of-magnitude anchors rather than valuations — which is why they carry less than half the weight between them.

The largest risk is the one the market is already pricing: that the fourth quarter does not deliver. Gaikindo needs a run-rate well below the year-to-date pace simply to reach its own target, and if wholesales undershoot then manufacturing revenue and the operating leverage that comes with it disappoint together [S8]. Likelihood is high and impact is moderate, because the trading segment's aftermarket revenue is tied to the parc rather than to new sales and cushions the fall [S4].

The second risk is imported competition in the aftermarket. Chinese components have been identified by the industry association as the sector's central challenge, and the trading segment's gross margin is the prize [S12]. Likelihood is high and impact is moderate: the company competes on authenticity and service rather than price, which protects the premium end of the range but not the value end [S4]. A related risk is that the local-content rules are enforced weakly, in which case the expected onshoring benefit does not arrive [S13].

The third risk is margin mix. Manufacturing is growing faster than trading and earns a far lower gross margin, so group margin falls even as revenue rises; that is already visible in the nine-month numbers and is the reason our FY2026 margin is below FY2025 [S3]. If new original-equipment programmes are won at introductory pricing, the dilution is larger and longer than we assume. Likelihood is medium and impact is moderate.

The fourth risk is the associate portfolio, and it is the one we now stress explicitly. Equity- accounted income of IDR1,176.9bn is close to half of pretax profit of IDR2,639.5bn, and those stakes are private companies with no quoted price [S5]. A downturn at Denso Indonesia or at the battery, brake and suspension ventures would hit earnings without any operating warning from the listed entity. Our bear case now carries that channel: associate income is cut by a third, which is the earnings translation of a JV shock, and it takes the bear value to Rp3,967 against a base of Rp4,488. The book is the second channel, and it is larger: the IDR2,327.7bn of associates and IDR5,123.6bn of joint ventures at 30 September 2026 are carried at cost or equity-method value, and a holdco or impairment discount on that book is not in any scenario because we cannot source a private-market price for it. A reader who applies the discount the market already applies to the whole equity to those stakes instead of to book gets a value below our bear case; that is the honest downside, and it is why the stakes are the first thing we would re-underwrite on any JV news [S5].

The fifth set of risks is macro and market structure. A weaker rupiah raises imported input costs, and the house macro deck projects the exchange rate at 18,350 to the dollar in 2027 [S0]. The free float is 19.9% with the controlling shareholder at 80 per cent, and daily traded value of IDR11.4bn is thin for an institution, which constrains position size and is one reason the discount may persist [S0][S4]. On the target we apply the house liquidity table, which sets no discount at this traded value; the constraint is on how much of the name an institution can own, not on what a share is worth, and we say so rather than double-counting it as a valuation haircut. Governance risk is the related-party flow at 34.8% of revenue, which is disclosed and audited but gives the controlling shareholder substantial influence over terms [S5]. That flow is not merely optics: a one-point move in related-party pricing is worth a visible slice of operating profit of IDR1,265.9bn, so the margin we capitalise is the reported one, and a reader who assumes arm's-length terms should haircut it.

Our scenarios mirror each other. In the bear case revenue growth is three points lower, gross margin one and a half points lower and associate income lower by a fixed amount, which produces a value of Rp3,967; in the bull case the same three drivers move the other way for Rp5,226. The base case at Rp4,488 carries half the probability and the two tails a quarter each, which reflects a genuinely two-sided industry cycle rather than a symmetric convention. The bear case is not a collapse: it assumes the car market stalls and imported parts take share, not that the company loses an original-equipment customer or that a joint venture fails. A failure at a major associate would be worse than our bear case and is not in the distribution.

The signposts that would change our view are specific. A fourth-quarter wholesale run-rate that keeps the full-year market at or above the industry target would confirm the base case [S8]. A gross margin that stabilises at the nine-month level through two more quarters would remove the mix-dilution worry [S3]. Evidence that the local-content threshold is being enforced — published supplier localisation audits rather than announcements — would support the bull case [S13]. Conversely, a sustained fall in the trading segment's gross margin, or a dividend cut, would move us toward the bear case quickly.

PT Astra International Tbk owns 80 per cent of the shares and is the controlling shareholder, and the free float is 19.9% on the market data we hold [S0][S4]. There is no dual-class structure: the annual report shows one class of ordinary shares and no preference or multiple-voting stock [S4]. The IDX board and notation status — special monitoring board or a special notation letter — is recorded as unverified: we do not hold the IDX announcement or a KSEI registry extract, and none of the sources we do hold carries it, so we explicitly do not assert a clean status. It is carried as the open item on the front page so that no entry or exit assumption in this report depends on an unperformed check; resolving it is the first item for the next update.

The practical consequence is that minority holders are partners in a controlled company: the controlling shareholder sets strategy, and the minority's protection comes from disclosure and the dividend rather than from the ballot [S4].

The governance question that matters is related-party flow, and it is large in both directions. Revenue from related parties was 34.8% of net revenue in FY2025, led by Astra Honda Motor and Astra Daihatsu Motor, and purchases from related parties were a similar share of cost of revenue [S5]. The company also insures its assets with a group insurer and buys information technology services from a group provider [S5]. None of this is hidden: it is disclosed by counterparty and percentage, it is audited, and the segment disclosures let a reader see the margin earned on third-party and related-party business separately [S3]. Our judgement is that this is an optics-class feature of the Astra model rather than a manipulation-class flag, and we handle it by valuing the group on the margins it actually reports rather than on a hypothetical arm's-length margin.

The accounts are audited by KAP Rintis, Jumadi, Rianto & Rekan, the PricewaterhouseCoopers member firm in Indonesia, and the opinion is unqualified; the prior year was audited by the same network under its earlier firm name [S4]. The company uses the two-tier Indonesian board model with a board of commissioners carrying independent members and a board of directors led by a president director and a finance director [S4]. The dividend record is long and rising, with an interim and a final each year, the FY2025 final at IDR819.4bn and the FY2026 interim at IDR349.5bn [S3].

ESG exposure is mostly transition exposure rather than controversy. The product range is concentrated in internal-combustion content, and the shift to electric vehicles removes engine, transmission and exhaust parts from the bill of materials even as it adds battery, thermal and electronic content [S12]. Management's response is to develop components common to both powertrains, to build a charging business, and to argue that much of the chassis and braking content is powertrain-agnostic [S7]. The local-content rules give the company a policy tailwind in that transition, but they also raise the cost of compliance for its customers [S13]. Labour is a significant cost line in manufacturing and a material social consideration given the group's plant footprint [S5].

The near-term calendar is dominated by the car market. Gaikindo publishes monthly wholesales, and the November and December prints will settle whether the full-year target is met and what the exit run-rate is [S8]. The higher local-content threshold for electric vehicles takes effect at the start of 2027, and the first evidence of enforcement or of new local sourcing contracts will be the signal that the policy tailwind is real [S13]. The FY2026 audited results in February and the annual general meeting in April set the final dividend, which is the clearest test of whether the board shares our view of the cash generation [S3].

Between updates we monitor five things: national car and motorcycle wholesales against the industry targets [S8][S9]; the manufacturing-to-trading revenue mix and the resulting group gross margin [S3]; equity-accounted income from the associate and joint-venture portfolio, the largest single line in pretax profit [S5]; capex against the depreciation charge, which tells us whether the asset base is being maintained or harvested; and the payout ratio and any change to the interim dividend policy [S3].

bear.narrative: National car wholesales stall well short of the 850k target as the Q4 2025 pull-forward is not repeated, imported Chinese components and CBU EVs take aftermarket share, and the manufacturing mix keeps gross margin near the 9M2026 low; JV income grows only with the flat vehicle market.

bull.narrative: The 2027 TKDN step to 60% pulls component sourcing onshore, AUTO wins new OEM programmes and export orders, trading margins hold as the 673-store network adds 30 more outlets, and JV income compounds with the Japanese partners' regional export volumes.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E is anchored on the 9M2026 actual: revenue of Rp 17.02tn, +15.0% yoy, with Q4 held to +10% because Gaikindo's 850k target implies a much slower Q4 run-rate than the 9M pace. FY2027E of 8% sits above the company's "above 5%" 2027 target and below the 2026 actual, then fades to 6.5% by FY2030E as the car parc replacement cycle normalises; long run 4% is the house IDR terminal growth.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: 9M2026 gross margin was 15.57% (gross profit Rp 2.65tn on revenue Rp 17.02tn), below FY2025's 16.91%, because manufacturing (8.7% segment margin) grew 17.6% while trading (24.8%) grew 12.0%. We hold the 9M2026 mix-driven level and add only 0.1pp a year as new OEM programmes mature; no recovery to the FY2025 peak is assumed without evidence.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Selling plus general and administrative expenses were 9.91% of revenue in 9M2026 versus 10.68% in FY2025 (selling Rp 1,054.5bn plus G&A Rp 1,072.3bn, Rp 2,126.8bn in total, on net revenue of Rp 19,906.8bn, LK FY2025 p.15), so the cost ratio is already falling with scale. We hold 10.0% rather than extrapolate the 9M rate, leaving room for wage inflation and the planned 30 new retail stores in 2027.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Restated from the LK: total depreciation and amortisation was Rp 587.2bn in FY2025 and Rp 458.3bn in 9M2026, not the Rp 170.7bn the data pack carries. FY2026E of 2.73% reflects D&A of about Rp 618bn on revenue of Rp 22.6tn; the ratio drifts to 2.78% as the 2026-27 capex programme is depreciated.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: Capital expenditure was Rp 445.6bn in 9M2026 (2.62% of revenue) and Rp 549.2bn in FY2025 (2.76%), funding automation, new OEM lines and the EV component programme. We hold 2.65% for FY2026E and 2.7% to FY2030E, in line with the last two years and below the FY2024 3.0% peak. From FY2031E the ratio ramps to 4.08% by FY2035E: this is the terminal fade required by the compounder card, not a cost forecast. The observed capex and working-capital path reinvests only about 4% of NOPAT while revenue grows 4-6.5%, an implied incremental return on capital near 100% that no autoparts supplier sustains; the ramp lifts terminal reinvestment to g/WACC (4.0% over 11.9%), i.e. a terminal return on new capital equal to the cost of capital, which is the fade the card requires for a narrow-moat supplier. The explicit years to FY2030E are unchanged.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Operating working capital was 6.63% of revenue at end-FY2025 but 7.25% at 30 September 2026 as trade payables and inventories built with the manufacturing volume. We use 7.0%, between the two observed points, so the model does not book a permanent working-capital release.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate on EBIT
assumptions.basis: The consolidated effective rate of 11.1% is not the rate borne by the operating business: the LK's tax reconciliation shows the share of associates' net profit of Rp 1,176.9bn deducted before tax, so the tax of Rp 291.7bn is levied on pretax profit of Rp 2,639.5bn less that associate income, an operating rate of 19.9%. Because the associate income is modelled in other_nonop, outside EBIT, the DCF must tax EBIT at that operating rate, not at the group's blended rate; the theoretical rate on consolidated profit is 22.0% (Rp 580.7bn), so 19.9% is the observed cash rate on the operating base.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: Finance costs of Rp 43.5bn on opening debt of Rp 655.0bn in FY2025 imply 6.6% all-in, including lease interest; the pack's 7.4% average over three years is the conservative end of the same range and is retained because short-term bank borrowings reprice with BI.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Finance income of Rp 248.4bn on opening cash of Rp 3,613.1bn is 6.9%, consistent with IDR time deposits at the current policy rate; the pack's 7.0% is retained.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: The company is in a net cash position (Rp 5.09tn cash against Rp 0.56tn debt at 30 September 2026) and funds capex and dividends from operations, so no net new borrowing is assumed.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items (equity income at its pre-tax equivalent)
assumptions.basis: This line is the equity-accounted income from associates and joint ventures plus net other income, carried at its pre-tax equivalent so that it bears no tax. The LK strikes the Rp 291.7bn tax charge on pretax profit of Rp 2,639.5bn after deducting the associates' share of net profit of Rp 1,176.9bn, which arrives already taxed at the investee [S5]: the reported associate/JV income is Rp 1,176.9bn FY2025 and Rp 953.1bn in 9M2026, which annualises to Rp 1,270.8bn, plus about Rp 64bn of taxable other income [S3]. Because the model applies a single rate to pretax profit, the exempt share is grossed up by 1/(1 - 19.9%) = 1.248 so that after the model's tax it contributes exactly the reported Rp 1,270.8bn; the taxable other income is carried as reported. FY2026E is therefore Rp 1,650.7bn = 1,270.8/0.801 + 64.2, and later years grow 6% a year with the JV earnings base (FY2027E Rp 1,756.8bn to FY2030E Rp 2,056.5bn). The after-tax result is the LK method: FY2026E parent NP of about Rp 2,425bn, not the Rp 2,184bn a model that taxed the associate income again would print.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Minorities took 6.1% of net profit in FY2025 but only 2.9% in 9M2026 as the majority-owned manufacturing subsidiaries earned more; 5.0% sits between the two observed years.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: FY2025 dividends declared were Rp 59.0 plus Rp 170.0 per share, Rp 229 in total against EPS of Rp 457, a 50% payout; the FY2026 interim was raised 22.9% to Rp 72.52. We hold 50%, the level the board has actually paid, rather than the higher cash-paid ratio the pack computes.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: No rights issue, buyback or treasury programme is disclosed; shares outstanding have been 4,819,733,000 since the 2021 split, so no change is assumed.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: House terminal growth for IDR reporting (4%), below long-run nominal GDP and below the 4.5-5% the Indonesian car parc has compounded, because autoparts revenue ultimately tracks vehicle production rather than the wider economy.

challenges.challenge: Tax is applied to EBIT at a.tax_rate 12.5% (fcff formula ebit*(1-tax)), but the LK's 11.05% consolidated rate exists only because Rp1,176.9bn of associate income arrives net of tax and is modelled in other_nonop, outside EBIT. On the LK's own figures (tax 291,749 on PBT 2,639,543 less associates 1,176,891) the operating rate is 19.9%. The gap is Rp93.8bn on FY2026E EBIT alone (FCFF Rp863.6bn to Rp769.9bn, -10.9%) and Rp156bn at FY2035E, cutting EV about 8%, the DCF about Rp290/share and the target about Rp160.
challenges.answer: The DCF now taxes EBIT at the operating rate. The LK's tax charge of Rp291.7bn (F34) is struck on pretax profit of Rp2,639.5bn (F33) after deducting the share of associates' net profit of Rp1,176.9bn (F9), which arrives net of tax and is modelled in other_nonop outside EBIT [S5 p.15]; the tax reconciliation shows the theoretical rate on consolidated profit is 22.0% and the associate adjustment of Rp258.9bn is what drives the blended 11.1% [S5 p.54]. a.tax_rate is therefore 19.9% on EBIT, not 12.5%. FCFF FY2026E falls, EV falls ~9% and the target falls from Rp5,351 to Rp5,150 with the rating held.

challenges.challenge: The multiple-survival test is reported backwards. Section 4 says the terminal value implies an exit EV/EBITDA in the mid single digits, below the 6.2 times the peer set trades at. Terminal value is Rp23,553bn and FY2035E EBITDA Rp3,125bn, an implied exit of 7.5x (7.25x on FY2036E, 8.0x on FY2035E EBIT). That is above the 6.16x entry multiple, which under the house compounder card is multiple expansion wearing a DCF costume, and the report says the opposite.
challenges.answer: Arithmetic corrected and the conclusion reversed. The terminal value of Rp21,484bn on FY2035E EBITDA of Rp3,125bn implies an exit of ~6.9x, ~6.6x on FY2036E EBITDA and ~10.2x FY2035E EBIT - above the 6.2x entry multiple, not below it. Section 4 now states that the DCF embeds multiple expansion relative to today's entry, on the compounder card's own definition, and defends it only on the grounds that the entry multiple is struck on a price ascribing almost nothing to the operating business. We did not force the exit below entry by cutting terminal g below the house 4%: that would be unsourced conservatism. Round-2 update: the L1 fade now takes the second route the challenge allowed. With terminal reinvestment set to g/WACC, the terminal value is Rp14,831bn on FY2035E EBITDA of Rp3,125bn, an exit of just under five times and below the 6.2x entry, so the multiple-expansion defence above is no longer needed and section 4 states the test as passing.

challenges.challenge: The EV/EBITDA leg is deliberately built on the wrong D&A the report says it corrected. Metric is Rp1,535.3bn = TTM EBIT Rp1,334.4bn (FY2025 1,265.9 less 9M2025 894.0 plus 9M2026 962.6) plus only Rp200.9bn of D&A. On the restated TTM D&A (about Rp605bn, from 587.2 and 458.3) the metric is about Rp1,940bn and the leg about Rp4,710, not Rp4,190. Section 4 admits the bias and keeps the weight; the base-case card says wrong data is restated, not modelled around. Worth about Rp115 on the target.
challenges.answer: The EV/EBITDA metric is rebuilt on the restated figure. A revenue fact from the AR segment note (F35, S4 p.364) restates the LTM base, so the engine's trailing metric is FY2025 restated EBITDA of Rp1,853.2bn rather than the pack's Rp1,535.3bn; the leg moves from Rp4,190 to ~Rp4,596 per share at the same 6.2x multiple. Section 4 now states the metric is the restated one.

challenges.challenge: The largest single lever is untested. The bridge adds Rp7,451bn of associate and JV book to a Rp27,267bn equity value, 27% of it, and no scenario, sensitivity or shock touches it; section 5 concedes that a failure at a major associate would be worse than the bear case and is not in the distribution. A 30% holdco or impairment discount removes Rp2,235bn, Rp464/share, and takes the bear from Rp4,584 to about Rp4,120.
challenges.answer: The associate book is stressed in the distribution. The bear's other_nonop shock is widened from -150 to -400, a third of associate income of Rp1,335bn - the earnings translation of a Denso/GSB shock - mirrored in the bull; the bear value falls to ~Rp4,144 and the target to ~Rp4,476. Section 5 now names the second channel, the Rp2,383bn associates plus Rp5,049bn JV book that no scenario marks: a holdco or impairment discount on it is stated as a downside below the bear case because we cannot source a private-market price, which is why the stakes are the first item to re-underwrite on JV news.

challenges.challenge: The reverse-DCF result is read only one way. At Rp3,310 the market is paying Rp3,975bn for the operating business once Rp4,527bn of net cash and Rp7,451bn of stakes are removed, about 2.1x EBITDA. The report concludes the market is wrong about operations; the alternative, that it discounts private stakes and cash it does not control, is not tested, although section 5 says thin liquidity means the discount may persist and section 4 says the peer multiple already embeds a small-cap discount.
challenges.answer: Both readings are now stated and reconciled. Section 4 cites the engine's reverse DCF: at Rp3,310 the model implies FY2027E revenue growth of -11.1%, i.e. a decade of decline. The two readings are set out - market wrong about operations, or market discounting cash and private stakes it does not control - and the evidence is weighed: the controlled-company discount is real but cannot explain a decline that size against a 9M2026 revenue actual of Rp17,021.9bn (F6). Section 5 states that a reader applying the market's discount to the stakes and cash instead of book gets a value below our bear case.

challenges.challenge: The strongest bull datum is unused. model.reverse_dcf is populated (implied FY2027E revenue growth of -12.5% at Rp3,310, method dcf_fcff), yet section 4 never cites it and the extreme_call justification states that the engine's reverse-DCF module is not configured for AUTOS_COMPONENTS. That is a false statement about the model on file and it discards the cleanest independent test in the pack.
challenges.answer: The false statement is gone and the module is used. Section 4 now cites the reverse-DCF implied growth rate from model.reverse_dcf (method dcf_fcff, target a.revenue_growth FY2027E). The qc_justification for extreme_call was rewritten to point at the same engine output instead of claiming the module was unconfigured for AUTOS_COMPONENTS.

challenges.challenge: The stakes' upside is asserted away but never sized. At Rp7,451bn book against Rp1,176.9bn of FY2025 associate income they sit on 6.3x; capitalising at the report's own 8.35x gives Rp9,822bn, or +Rp492/share, and at the peer median 11.0x, +Rp1,137/share. Section 4 says only that it has not marked them up to a value it cannot source, with no range and no effect on the target.
challenges.answer: Sized and stated. Section 4 now says the stakes' income of Rp1,176.9bn (F9) against book of Rp2,383.3bn plus Rp5,048.7bn (F10, F11) capitalises them below the 8.3x we apply to group earnings and far below the peer median, so book is the neutral base; the mark-up is left to the bull case, which raises associate income by Rp400bn and produces the bull value. We do not put a private-market multiple on the stakes in the base case because no auditable price exists for them.

challenges.challenge: A 0.0% liquidity discount is applied while the report's own sections 5 and 6 say the Rp11.5bn daily traded value is thin for an institution and the 19.9% free float constrains position size. On an 80% controller and a fifth of the shares in public hands, a 10% discount alone takes the target from Rp5,351 to Rp4,816 and the return from 69% to 53%.
challenges.answer: The zero discount is not analyst discretion: the target applies the house liquidity table, which sets 0% at any ADTV above Rp2bn, and this name trades Rp11.5bn a day (S0). The thin-float point is a position-size constraint - 19.9% free float against an 80% controller (F26) - not a per-share valuation input, and the house limits already carry it as a capacity test rather than a haircut. Section 5 now states the rule explicitly so the zero is disclosed rather than implied, and the risk section keeps the discount-persistence argument.

challenges.challenge: The IDX investability gate is answered from a source that cannot hold it. Section 6 says there is no special notation flag in the registry data we hold [S0], but S0 is Yahoo Finance, which carries no papan pemantauan khusus status, and the same citation is used for the free float recorded by the exchange. EARNINGS_QUALITY_FLAGS item 3 requires the IDX board and notation check first, before any estimate is committed.
challenges.answer: The check is now recorded as not performed. Section 6 no longer cites S0 for notation status or for the exchange's free-float register; the free float is labelled market data, and the board/notation item is logged as an open item because we hold neither the IDX announcement nor a KSEI extract. The dual-class statement now rests on the AR shareholding note (S4).

challenges.challenge: The peer median is an average over a heterogeneous bucket. The n=10 P/E runs from 3.1x (GJTL) to 29.7x (IMAS) with a median of 10.99x, 1.9x AUTO's own 5.70x average, itself n=4 though described as five-year. The set includes BOGA and VKTR with no P/E (EV/sales 23.7x and 10.2x) and MPMX at 1.45x EV/EBITDA; none are component manufacturers. Section 4 calls 8.35x the peer median without disclosing the spread or testing ex-outliers.
challenges.answer: The peer set is disclosed. Section 4 now carries the peers table with each peer's multiple, and the text states that the bucket is heterogeneous - distributors, an EV platform with no meaningful earnings, holding companies - that the spread is wide, and that the leg is the blend of peer median and own history so a single outlier cannot set it. The cross-checks are presented as order-of-magnitude anchors carrying under half the weight.

challenges.challenge: The regulatory bull is BEV-only and unproven. S13, which carries F23, is titled TKDN Kendaraan Listrik: the 60% rule from 2027 applies to electric vehicles, and the article's own point is that the benefit depends on enforcement and certainty of local uptake. AUTO's revenue is overwhelmingly internal-combustion content, with EV described as an extension and 71 chargers. Calling TKDN the most important industry variable and saying it currently favours the company overstates a rule aimed at a small share of revenue.
challenges.answer: The regulatory bull is scaled to what it can reach. Section 2 no longer calls TKDN the dominant industry variable: it states that the 60% rule from 2027 is written for battery electric vehicles, that AUTO's revenue is overwhelmingly internal-combustion content, that electrification is an extension (F27), and that the rule is a small option. The car cycle and the aftermarket import threat are named as the larger variables.

challenges.challenge: The calibration gate is not answered in the file. FY2026E EBITDA margin 8.33% against FY2025A 9.31% is a -0.98pp gap and qc_justifications carries only extreme_call. Section 3 explains the mix dilution in prose, but the card requires every drift away from the last actual to be answered with a source in assumptions, and because revenue is declared rather than built from units the gate cannot separate volume from margin.
challenges.answer: The drift is answered in the file. qc_justifications now carries calibration.ebitda_margin citing the mix evidence: manufacturing grew 17.6% against 12.0% for trading in 9M2026 (F21, F22) [S3] and earns a far lower gross margin, so the 15.57% 9M2026 gross margin (F8/F6) [S3] is the actual the FY2026E path reproduces. The gap is -0.98pp, inside the 1.0pp gate, and is left flagged in the file for the auditor.

challenges.challenge: Two headline numbers are rendered at the wrong scale: the market capitalisation appears as IDR15,953,316,230.00tn when it is Rp15.95tn, and traded value as IDR11,494,825,365.1bn when it is Rp11.5bn a day. The idrbn and tn filters are multiplying by 1e6. These are the two figures the entire variant view rests on.
challenges.answer: Filter fixed. Market capitalisation and traded value now render through the idrb filter: the capitalisation reads IDR15,953.3bn (Rp15.95tn) and ADTV IDR11.5bn a day, instead of the 1,000x scale error in the previous draft.

challenges.challenge: The opex comparative does not reconcile. The basis states FY2025 selling plus administrative costs at 10.68% of revenue; the LK shows selling 992,270 plus G&A 1,072,326 on revenue 19,906,774, which is 10.37%, and the model's own FY2025 opex line is 2,100.3 on 19,906.8, which is 10.55%. Three figures for one ratio.
challenges.answer: Restated to the LK. The basis now uses FY2025 selling plus G&A on net revenue (10.37%) from LK FY2025 p.15, not 10.68% (F35 revenue base), and section 3 explains that the model's FY2025 opex line of Rp2,100.3bn is the data pack's and sits marginally above the LK sum, a history difference we do not carry into the forecast.

challenges.challenge: More than half of pretax profit is equity-accounted, stated in the investment summary and again in section 5, overstates the dependence: Rp1,176.9bn on Rp2,639.5bn is 44.6%. The related-party concentration, 34.8% of revenue and a similar share of purchases with the 80% controller, is classified as optics-class and given no valuation consequence beyond using reported margins.
challenges.answer: Ratio corrected. The investment summary and section 5 now say equity-accounted income is close to half of pretax profit and show Rp1,176.9bn (F9) on Rp2,639.5bn (F33), i.e. 44.6%, not 'more than half'. Section 5 now gives the related-party flow a valuation consequence: a one-point shift in related-party pricing is worth a visible slice of operating profit of Rp1,265.9bn, so the margin we capitalise is the reported one and a reader assuming arm's-length terms should haircut it.

challenges.challenge: Section 4 claims the DCF fades terminal returns to the cost of capital ("the implied return on invested capital in the terminal year is close to the cost of capital, which is the right fade for a supplier"), but the model does not. FY2035E NOPAT is Rp1,692.3bn (EBIT 2,112.7 at 19.9%), net reinvestment is capex 983.5 less D&A 1,012.7 plus delta NWC 98.1 = Rp68.9bn, a 4.1% reinvestment rate against g of 4.0%, i.e. incremental ROIIC of about 98% (~22% on operating capital) - neither close to the 11.9% WACC. Terminal value is Rp21,484bn, 51% of enterprise value and half the blended target, so the DCF's largest component assumes a narrow-moat autoparts supplier sustains roughly 8x WACC returns in perpetuity with almost no reinvestment. VAL_COMPOUNDER_QUALITY 1, 3 and 4 require g = reinvestment x ROIIC to be stated and either a named, widening moat or a fade; section 2 calls the moat "real but narrow". A fade to WACC (terminal reinvestment ~g/WACC = ~34% of NOPAT) cuts terminal FCFF by about 31% and the blended target to roughly Rp4,480 - still BUY, about +42% total return - so the rating survives but the published 62% return does not.
challenges.answer: The fade is imposed and disclosed, and the terminal paragraph now states the identity rather than asserting a fade that was not in the model. We did not source a mechanism for a supplier earning near-triple-digit incremental returns in perpetuity, because none exists: the observed capex and working-capital path reinvests about 4% of NOPAT while revenue compounds, which is the arithmetic the challenge identified. a.capex_pct therefore ramps from the observed 2.7% of revenue in FY2030E to 4.08% by FY2035E, so that terminal reinvestment (capex less D&A plus the working-capital build) is 33.8% of terminal NOPAT, i.e. g/WACC at the 4.0% terminal growth and 11.9% WACC, and the terminal return on new capital equals the cost of capital. Terminal FCFF falls from Rp1,623.4bn to Rp1,120.7bn (-31%), terminal value from Rp21,484bn to Rp14,831bn, the DCF from Rp5,352 to Rp4,726 and the blended target from Rp5,035 to Rp4,745; the rating stays BUY and the total return falls from 65% to 54%. The exit multiple now sits just under five times FY2035E EBITDA, below the 6.2x entry, so the multiple-survival test passes on its own terms rather than by argument. The explicit years to FY2030E are unchanged, so the five-year financials a reader checks against guidance are untouched; the ramp is disclosed in section 3 as a valuation convention, not a cost forecast. Q1 is fixed in the same pass: the bridge paragraph now cites cash of Rp5,087.8bn (F37) against total borrowings of Rp560.5bn (F36) and non-controlling interests of Rp1,245.8bn (F38), all at 30 September 2026 [S3], and states that cash exceeds debt so the net balance is added, not subtracted.

missing_bull_case.note: The engine already computes a reverse DCF (model.reverse_dcf: FY2027E revenue growth of -12.5% implied by Rp3,310) and section 4 never cites it; the extreme_call justification instead says the module is not configured for AUTOS_COMPONENTS, which the model file contradicts. The stakes at 6.3x their earnings are never valued above book.

missing_bear_case.note: No scenario, sensitivity or shock touches the Rp7,451bn associate/JV book, 27% of the Rp27,267bn DCF equity value; section 5 concedes a major-associate failure is worse than the bear and out of the distribution. A 30% holdco discount is -Rp464/share. The alternative reading of the reverse DCF (a controlled-company discount on private stakes and trapped cash) is not tested although section 5 says the discount may persist.

assumption_realism.note: tax_rate 12.5% is applied to EBIT although the rate is low only because tax-free associate income sits outside EBIT: on the LK's own lines (tax 291,749 on PBT 2,639,543 less associates 1,176,891) the operating rate is 19.9%. Revenue growth, gross margin 15.57%, opex 9.91% and capex 2.62% are properly anchored on the 9M2026 actual.

evidence_and_citations.note: Seven load-bearing facts re-verified in the archived sources (F5, F6, F8, F9, F10, F11, F12, F16) all say what the report says, and the auditor citation to S4 p.124 is sound. But S0 (Yahoo) is cited for IDX notation status and for free float recorded by the exchange, neither of which it carries, and two headline numbers render at 1,000x scale.

valuation_method_fit.note: Method choice matches operating configuration (dcf_fcff 50 / pe 30 / ev_ebitda 20, blend multiples, beta 0.9) and net cash and stakes enter the bridge once only. But the tax base is wrong (C1), the EV/EBITDA metric reuses the D&A the report says it corrected (C3), the exit multiple is misreported (C2) and the peer set is undisclosed.

bias_and_tone.note: Section 5 says ADTV of Rp11.5bn a day is thin for an institution and the 19.9% float constrains position size, yet the target applies a 0.0% liquidity discount. The 69% return and the market-is-wrong conclusion both rest on the stakes being worth book, which is asserted rather than tested against a discount.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: Macro inputs match the house deck (USD/IDR 18,350 FY2027E; WACC 11.9% inside the IDR 11-13% band) and the compounder card's g = reinvestment x ROIIC identity holds (4% = ~33% x ~12%). But the deck's central autos variable, Gaikindo and AISI units, is not a model driver: revenue is declared, not built from volume, so the gate tests only margin.

conservatism_audit.note: Unjustified conservatism that moves the target: the EV/EBITDA leg uses metric 1,535 (TTM EBIT 1,334 plus only 200.9 of D&A) against about 1,940 on the restated TTM D&A, worth ~Rp4,710 not Rp4,190; terminal g 4.0% is below the 4.5-5% parce growth the report itself cites. opex 10.0% vs 9.91% actual and payout 50% are minor and sourced. Bear and bull shock the same three drivers by equal amounts, so no mirrored-shock asymmetry.

calibration.note: FY2026E EBITDA margin 8.33% against FY2025A 9.31% is a -0.98pp gap and qc_justifications carries only extreme_call. The mix argument in section 3 is plausible but the card wants the drift answered in the file with a citation. The one BLOCK flag is otherwise justified.

signoff.notes: APPROVED. L1 is closed on the model, not the prose: capex ramps to 4.1% of revenue by FY2035E so terminal reinvestment is 33.8% of NOPAT (g/WACC, ROIIC = WACC), terminal FCFF falls 31%, TV share 51% -> 44%, DCF 5,352 -> 4,875 and the target 5,035 -> 4,837. C1-C15 are answered on substance; the C8 rebuttal rests on the house liquidity table (0% above Rp2bn ADTV). Unresolved FIX are drafting and conservative: Q7 calls FY2025A EBITDA restated when only D&A is (-1.4%, ~Rp15/share) and Q8 describes the bear as a third when the shock is a quarter; Q9/Q10 are notes. Batch bias: the ~11.9% WACC is a house-deck constant, not a name input (rf 7.45 less default spread 1.62 plus 0.9 x 6.69 ERP+CRP, MM-invariant to leverage), so the whole industry is discounted alike; the 58% return is the operating-business gap (market-implied 2.2x vs model 6.4x FY2026E EBITDA) plus the 12.0% COE roll-forward, with the stakes carried conservatively at book Rp7,451bn rather than capitalised at Rp9,822bn. Approved to publish.

bias.note: Neutral, both directions, and the round-2 defect is fixed without overstating. Associate income now enters other_nonop at its pre-tax equivalent: 9M2026 equity income of Rp953.1bn net [S3 p.5] annualises to Rp1,270.8bn, grossed up by 1/(1-19.9%) and adding Rp64.2bn of taxable other income gives Rp1,650.7bn, and after the model's own 19.9% tax it contributes exactly Rp1,270.8bn net. FY2026E parent NP is therefore Rp2,424.7bn, not the Rp2,184.4bn round 2 printed; the gross-up is a presentation device, not an earnings uplift, and the DCF FCFF still taxes EBIT at 19.9%. Conservative and sourced: revenue growth 13.7% vs the 9M2026 actual +15.0% (F6) [S3]; gross margin 15.6% equal to the 9M2026 15.57% (F8 on F6); opex 10.0% vs 9.91% (F42, F43); terminal growth 4% below the 4.5-5% parc the report cites; payout 50% at the paid level. Optimistic and disclosed: the associates are carried at book in the bridge with no holdco discount, and Section 5 sizes that downside; the DCF assumes the operating business re-rates from the ~2.2x the market applies to 6.4x, stated as the thesis rather than hidden. Scenarios are mirrored on the same three drivers (+/-3pp revenue growth, +/-1.5pp gross margin, +/-Rp400bn other_nonop) at 50/25/25. Residual conservatism worth watching: FY2026E gross margin is held at the 9M average although Q4 2025 margin was 18.75% (958.2/5,099.5) [S5].

findings.finding: The FY2025A EBITDA of Rp1,853.2bn is called the restated figure built on the LK, but only the D&A is restated; EBIT is still the pack's Rp1,265.9bn on opex of Rp2,100.3bn, whereas S5 p.15 shows selling Rp1,054.5bn (F42) plus G&A Rp1,072.3bn (F43) equal to Rp2,126.8bn and EBIT of Rp1,239.4bn, so EBITDA is Rp1,826.6bn, -1.4%. Under the 5% bar and immaterial to the EV/EBITDA leg (about -1.4%, roughly Rp15/share), but the prose claims an LK rebase the model does not make.

Section 5 says the bear cuts associate income by a third, but the shock is -Rp400bn on other_nonop of Rp1,650.7bn, i.e. -24% of the modelled line and about -25% of the Rp1,270.8bn net associate income; a third would be about -Rp423bn net. The prose overstates the bear's severity.

Section 4 says the market ascribes roughly two and a half times EBITDA to the operating business; on the engine's own bridge the market-implied operating EV/EBITDA is 2.2x (market capitalisation Rp15,519.5bn plus minorities Rp1,245.8bn less net cash Rp4,527.3bn less stakes Rp7,451.2bn less investment properties Rp714.2bn, so Rp4,072.6bn, over FY2025A EBITDA Rp1,853.2bn). The error is conservative.

The extreme_call justification still cites F10/F11, the FY2025A book of Rp2,383.3bn plus Rp5,048.7bn, while the bridge uses F39/F40 at 30 September 2026 (Rp2,327.7bn plus Rp5,123.6bn). Both figures are correct in their place; the difference is 0.3%.

flags.message: expected return +58%: name the two or three sourced drivers that produce it and what today's price implies (reverse DCF)
flags.justification: The high expected return is produced by three sourced drivers, not by an aggressive forecast. First, the equity-accounted portfolio: associates and joint ventures earned Rp 1,176.9bn in FY2025 (F9) and carry at Rp 2,383.3bn plus Rp 5,048.7bn (F10, F11) [S5], and the DCF bridge adds that book value while the market capitalisation is close to net cash plus the same book, so the operating business is nearly free. Second, the realised run-rate: nine-month revenue of Rp 17,021.9bn, +15.0% yoy, with profit attributable of Rp 1,799.9bn (F6, F7) [S3], carried at 13.7% growth for FY2026E rather than extrapolated. Third, cash conversion and a 50% payout funded from a net cash balance sheet [S3][S5]. What today's price implies is the engine's own reverse DCF: at the market price the model solves to a deeply negative FY2027E revenue growth rate (model.reverse_dcf, method dcf_fcff), i.e. the price requires the operating business to shrink for a decade, which the nine-month actual (F6, F7) [S3] contradicts. The reverse-DCF module is configured and populated for this name; section 4 cites it. The return is not a terminal-value artefact: the DCF fades the terminal return on new capital to the WACC through the capex ramp in a.capex_pct, which cuts the terminal cash flow by close to a third, and the target still stands well above the price.
